title: Philanthropy as Continuation
author: RN Collins
principle: Evidence leads; atmosphere never substitutes for provenance.

narrativeSequence.caption: Philanthropic continuation is strongest when it funds the conditions for new creators to build authority—not when it requires them to reproduce a founder’s style or gratitude.
A commercial name can identify the business presented to buyers while the image itself preserves a different maker attribution.
narrativeSequence.rights: Free to Use and Reuse / Library of Congress curated set

narrativeSequence.caption: 01 · CONDITION — Which barrier is being changed?. Use participant and field evidence to name the constraint—time, space, tools, care, legal access, production, archive, education, market, or safety—without inventing deficit narratives.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery

narrativeSequence.caption: 02 · POWER — Who defines success?. Allocate governance among participants, practitioners, community authorities, staff, independent reviewers, and funder; disclose conflicts and create appeal and correction routes.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery

narrativeSequence.caption: 03 · RIGHT — What do recipients retain?. Separate grant conditions, IP, name and likeness, documentation, data, confidentiality, cultural knowledge, publication, archive, and post-program access.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery

narrativeSequence.caption: 04 · CONTINUE — What remains when funding stops?. Plan unrestricted assets, maintained tools, open or governed curricula, participant networks, preserved records, successor funding, and an ethical closure route.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery
